messages.author: 33d5534e21fbbe0f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: specifying initial values for vb in rstan - can't get ADVI model to run
parts:
Thx for the quick reply, Ben.  I hadn't thought about the point that initial values are generated for unconstrained parameters under mean-field Gaussian estimation.  I tried both limiting the range with init_r (e.g., init_r = 1) but receive the same error messages I specified in my first email.  Does the failure to generate acceptable initial values indicate that normal approximations for one or more of the parameters in the unconstrained space don't work?  Seems counterintuitive as my model is a mixture of Gaussians.  Is it common to have one's ADVI estimation fail on generation of the initial values?  I use weakly informative priors.  I'm not getting any traction by further tightening these priors - I get the same errors, not matter how informative I make the priors.  Lastly, it is a problem to use restricted specifications, such a cov_matrix and cholesky_factor_cov - I do get an "informational' message" that a cholesky_factor_cov in my model is ill-conditioned.  When I increase init_r to a relatively large value (init_r = 10), I then receive a  further lack of symmetry message for the cholesky_factor_cov matrix.

I'm pretty well stuck as to how/whether to proceed with ADVI.

Terrance

On Tue, Jan 12, 2016 at 6:19 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
It is not currently possible to specify initial values for ADVI via rstan because the mechanism we use for sampling is not directly applicable since ADVI needs initial values for the normal variational approximation. You can however specify init_r to some value (it is 2 by default) to limit the range of the initial values in the variational approximation. I don't think the fact that you do Kronecker products or other operations make the evaluation of the log-posterior function too complicated, but it is a valid empirical question as to whether the parameters are approximately normal in the unconstrained space.

Ben


On Tuesday, January 12, 2016 at 6:00:38 PM UTC-5, tds151 wrote:
Hi, I'm attempting to perform ADVI on a mixture model in specified in the attached file, dpmix_2.stan.  The model imposes the mixture distribution on observation-indexed random effects, rather than directly on the (multivariate) data.  The mixture probabilities are specified such that limiting mixture distribution is a Dirichlet process (which penalizes the number of clusters selected).  The number of dimensions is relatively small, so cluster-indexed covariance matrices are included to allow the data to learn dependence among the dimensions.  The dimensions index time, so an autocorrelated covariance structure (CAR) is used.  Each multivariate observation is drawn from a Gaussian with the mean defined as the sum of a fixed effects term and an observation-indexed random effects term.

The attached file, syndata_vb_run.R uses draw_syndata_mix.R to generate synthetic data, then compiles the dpmix_2.stan to stanmodel object and performs ADVI estimation.  

I receive the following error message when running vb():

Rejecting initial value:
  Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value.

I'm also informed that:
   validate transformed params: Lbeta is not lower triangular; Lbeta[1,2]=1.62024e-315

the object Lbeta is the cholesky of a separable covariance matrix composed from the kronecker product of two lower dimensional covariance matrices.  everything is declared as restricted; e.g., cov_matrix, cholesky_factor_cov.

I'd appreciate your insight on the following questions:
1. Does this error message indicate that I should supply initial parameter values and, if so, how does one do that under vb() in rstan 2.9.0 (which i installed from github, yesterday)?
-- it seems vb() inputs a stanmodel object, but no input field for initial values

2. I'm using 3 x 3 and 12 x 12 covariance and precision matrices, separately, and built into a 36 x 36 separable covariance structure using the kronecker product.  Is this not a good idea for ADVI?  Said differently, is this model just too complicated for ADVI (at this time)?  I had hoped that my twist on the mixture model included in the paper was relatively minor.

3. Are there other considerations I should be aware of when assessing whether my model is estimable under ADVI?

Thank you for your help and expertise,

Terrance.

messages.author: 33d5534e21fbbe0f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: specifying initial values for vb in rstan - can't get ADVI model to run
parts:
Hi, I was able to get vb() launched by removing the restricted declaration, cholesky_factor_cov (for matrix Lbeta).   (As an aside, Stan's implementation of a restriction as a check contrasts with the Armadillo library's implementation to enforce - for numerical stability).   The vb() generally works *great* on this model, which has some complexity.  There is, however, some estimation bias (elicited by estimating the model on synthetic) data for the tau[k] parameters, which are CAR precision parameters, and I suspect I may not have a sufficient number of time points to well-estimate them (rather than the issue being the ADVI approximation).  So i'd like to check this by sampling() under NUTS for this model.  Yet, sampling() doesn't move past the first warm-up iteration.  I receive no messages (other than it is at iteration 1/2000 of chain 1).  All to say, the model script is listed, below, and I appreciate any insights you'd offer about how I might change it to get the NUTS sampler to move.  Thanks.

/*
  y[i] ~ N_{T}(B'x[i] + u[i], sigma_y),  where sigma_y are known
  B    ~ 0 + N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q^{-1})
  Q    = (D - rb*Omega) - a proper CAR construction without precision param for identifiability
  rb   ~ U(0,1)
  Lambda = diag(lam_tau) * corr_Lambda * diag(lam_tau), of dimension P x P
  lam_tau ~ cauchy(0,5)
  corr_Lambda ~ lkj(4)
  u[i] ~ prod_{k=1}^{K} theta[k] * N_{T}(0,mu[k],invSigma[k]^{-1}),
  invSigma[k]  = tau[k] * (D - rho[k]*Omega)
  mu[k,j] ~ N(0,5)
  tau[k]  ~ Gamma(1,1)
  rho[k]  ~ U(0,1)
  theta   ~ Dirichlet(alpha/K), which limits to a DP mixture

*/

functions{
    // sum a matrix, by rows
    vector row_sums(matrix X) 
    {
      vector[rows(X)] s ;  
      s <- X * rep_vector(1, cols(X)) ;
      return s;
    }
    
    // V \kron U
    matrix kron(matrix U, matrix V, int P, int T)
    {
      // U is P x P and V is T x T
      // result VU = V \kron U
      // so P is fast and T is slow
      matrix[P*T,P*T] VU;
      for(ti in 1:T)
        for(tj in 1:T)
          for(ni in 1:P)
            for(nj in 1:P)
              VU[P*(ti-1)+ni, P*(tj-1)+nj] <- V[ti,tj] * U[ni,nj];
      return VU;
    }
    
    // Convert an NT x 1 vector to an N x T matrix, by column
    matrix vec_to_mat(vector v, int N, int T)
    {
      // Fill, by column, so N is fast and T is slow 
      matrix[N,T] V;
      for( j in 1:T ) /* fill by column */
      {
        for( i in 1:N )
        {
          V[i,j] <- v[(N*(j-1)+i)];
        }
      }
      return V;
    }
    
} /* end user functions{} block */


data{
  int<lower=1> N; // number of domains
  int<lower=1> K; // *maximum* - truncated number of clusters
  int<lower=1> T; // number of times points - months
  int<lower=1> P; // number of predictors
  row_vector[T] y[N]; // Set of N, T x 1 multivariate observations
  row_vector<lower=0>[T] sigma_y[N]; // known area standard deviations
  matrix[N,P] x; // matrix of predictors
  matrix<lower=0>[T,T] Omega; // T x T CAR adjacency matrix for prior on cluster centers
} /* end data block */
  

transformed data{
  vector<lower=0>[K] ones_K;
  vector<lower=0>[T] d;
  matrix[T,T] D;
  ones_K <- rep_vector(1,K); /* dirichlet prior on alpha has equal shapes */
  d <- row_sums(Omega); /* diagonal entries of precision matrix */
  D <- diag_matrix(d);
} /* end transformed data block */

parameters{
  row_vector[T] u[N]; /* latent random effects receiving Gaussian mixture prior */
  simplex[K] theta; /* mixture probabilities after marginalizing over inclusions*/
  row_vector[T] mu[K]; /* cluster centers */
  real<lower=0> tau[K]; /* cluster precision parameters for T x T Rw(1) CAR precision matrix */
  real<lower=0,upper=1> rho[K]; /* cluster strength of correlation parameters */
  real alpha; /* DP concentration parameter */
  //real<lower=0> tb; /* precision parameter for T x T, Q, precision matrix for rows of Beta */
  real<lower=0,upper=1> rb; /* strength of correlation parameter */
  /* parameters to form P x P covariance matrix, Lambda, of B ~ 0 + N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q) */
  corr_matrix[P] corr_Lambda; /* correlation matrix for columns of Beta */
  vector<lower=0>[P] lam_tau; /* vector of sd parameters for P x P, Lambda */
  /* PT x 1, z ~ N(0,1), Lbeta <- chol(kron(Lambda,inv(Q)), beta_long <- Lbeta * z */
  /* equivalent to B ~ 0 + N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q) */
  vector[P*T] z;
} /* end parameters block */

transformed parameters{
  vector[P*T] beta_long; /* P is the fast index, T is the slow index */
  matrix[P,T] Beta;
  cov_matrix[P] Lambda;
  cov_matrix[T] Q;
  cov_matrix[P*T] Sig_beta; /* Sig_beta <- kron(Lambda,inv(Q)) = Q \kron Lambda */
  //cholesky_factor_cov[P*T] Lbeta;
  matrix[P*T,P*T] Lbeta;
  cov_matrix[T] invSigma[K]; /* invSigma[k] <- tau[k] * (D-rho[k]*Omega) */
  /* P x P covariance matrix, Lambda for cols of Beta */
  /* formed from correlation matrix, corr_Lambda, and std deviations, lam_tau */
  Lambda                    <- quad_form_diag( corr_Lambda, lam_tau );
  /* T x T precision matrix, Q, for rows of T x 1 rows of Beta */
  //Q                         <- tb * (D - rb * Omega);
  Q                         <- (D - rb * Omega);
  /* Implement a Beta ~ 0 + N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q^{-1}) by using  */
  /* beta_long ~ N_{PT}(0,Sig_beta), where Sig_beta = inverse(Q) \kron Lambda */
  /* Accomplish by generating PT x 1, z ~ N(0,1) */
  /* and forming beta_long <- Lbeta * z */
  /* where Lbeta = chol(Sig_beta) */
  Sig_beta                  <- kron(Lambda,inverse(Q),P,T);
  Lbeta                     <- cholesky_decompose( Sig_beta );
  /* P x T fixed effects, Beta, formed by re-shaping PT x 1, beta_long */
  beta_long                 <- Lbeta * z; // Beta ~ 0+ N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q)
  Beta                      <- vec_to_mat(beta_long,P,T); /* P is fast, T is slow */
  /* Construct set of K (cluster-indexed) T x T CAR precision matrices, invSigma */
  /* for mixture distribution for N x T, u */
  for( k in 1:K )
  {
    invSigma[k]               <- tau[k] * (D - rho[k] * Omega); 
  }
  
} /* end transformed parameters block */

model{
  // priors for mean and covariance cluster locations
  alpha ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 ); /* DP concentration parameter */
  theta ~ dirichlet( alpha/K * ones_K ); // instantiate a truncated DP prior
  { /* local variable block for invSigma[k] */
    /* priors for invSigma[k] */
    tau ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 ); /* K x 1 vector of cluster-indexed precision parameters */
    rho ~ uniform( 0, 1 ); /* K x 1 vector of cluster-indexed strength of correlation */
    for( k in 1:K )
    {
      mu[k]         ~ normal( 0.0, 5.0 ); /* T x 1 cluster centers */
    
    } /* end loop k over clusters */
  } /* end construction of local variables, invSigma */
  
   
  // prior for latent response, u_{i} ~ prod_{k=1}^{K}theta_k *N(u_{i},mu_k,Sigma_k)
  for( i in 1:N ) /* by row of N x T, u */
  {
    real ps[K];
    for( k in 1:K )
    {
      ps[k] <- log(theta[k]) + multi_normal_prec_log(u[i], mu[k], invSigma[k]);
    }
    increment_log_prob( log_sum_exp(ps) );
  }
  
  // prior for time-indexed fixed effects, P x T, Beta
  // using separable covariance structure with PxP Lambda
  // and TxT precision, Q (constructed as a CAR, RW(1))
  /* sample parameters that compose PxP, Lambda and TxT Q */
  { 
    /* TxT, Q <- tb * (D-rb*Omega) = CAR precision matrix */
    //tb                        ~ gamma( 1, 1 );
    rb                        ~ uniform( 0, 1 );
    
    // prior on P x P covariance matrix, Lambda 
    corr_Lambda               ~ lkj_corr( 4 );
    lam_tau                   ~ cauchy( 0, 5 );
    // note: kron(Lambda,Q) \ equiv Q \kron Lambda, so T is slow and P is fast.
    // results from stacking the columns of P x T, Beta into PT x 1, beta_long
    z                         ~ normal( 0,1 );
  } /* end local variable blocks for Q, Sigma_beta and Lbeta */
  
  
  // observed response likelihood
  { /* block to declare xb as a local variable */
    matrix[N,T] xb;
    xb    <- x * Beta; // N x P, x, times P x T, Beta
    for( i in 1:N ) /* by row of y */
    {
      y[i] ~ normal( xb[i] + u[i], sigma_y[i] ); /* vectorized for T x 1 response, y[i] */
    }
  } /* end block to declare xb as a local variable */
  
  
} /* end model{} block */

I'm not sure what you mean here --- I'm not familiar with
Armadillo.

> The vb() generally works *great* on this model, which has some complexity. There is, however, some estimation bias (elicited by estimating the model on synthetic) data for the tau[k] parameters, which are CAR precision parameters, and I suspect I may not have a sufficient number of time points to well-estimate them (rather than the issue being the ADVI approximation). So i'd like to check this by sampling() under NUTS for this model. Yet, sampling() doesn't move past the first warm-up iteration. I receive no messages (other than it is at iteration 1/2000 of chain 1). All to say, the model script is listed, below, and I appreciate any insights you'd offer about how I might change it to get the NUTS sampler to move. Thanks.

Presumably that'd be because it's trying to evaluate many leapfrog
steps. If you can give it a good starting point and if the variables
are all scaled similarly, it'll really help to get things moving.

Thanks for the tips, Bob.  I'm re-jiggering initial values and prior formulations as a model that estimates well under mean field vb() may not under NUTS.  I was wondering whether you would offer any insights on whether any of my prior formulations are particularly bad.  Yes, I know about the scaling issues, which defeated my previous attempts to estimate models in Stan with many levels of hierarchy.  

Armadillo is a C++ linear algebra library made available for use in R programming with Rcpp via the package RcppArmadillo.  It relies on the user's rblas, unlike RcppEigen used by Stan, but has easy-to-use syntax.  My point was that Armadillo also allows for restrictive declarations, which it enforces, to either employ a speedier decomposition algorithm or to aid in numerical stability.  So, for example, if one declares a matrix as lower triangular, it automatically zeros out the upper triangular elements.  Stan, differently, checks and may produce an error if any of the upper triangular elements of a declared cholesky covariance matrix are non-zero within some precision, which sometimes happens for me due to numerical precision issues.

>   /* P x T fixed effects, Beta, formed by re-shaping PT x 1, beta_long */
>   beta_long                 <- Lbeta * z; // Beta ~ 0+ N_{PxT}(Lambda,Q)
>   Beta                      <- vec_to_mat(beta_long,P,T); /* P is fast, T is slow */
>   /* Construct set of K (cluster-indexed) T x T CAR precision matrices, invSigma */
>   /* for mixture distribution for N x T, u */
>   for( k in 1:K )
>   {
>     invSigma[k]               <- tau[k] * (D - rho[k] * Omega);
>   }
>
> } /* end transformed parameters block */
>
> model{
>   // priors for mean and covariance cluster locations
>   alpha ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 ); /* DP concentration parameter */
>   theta ~ dirichlet( alpha/K * ones_K ); // instantiate a truncated DP prior
>   { /* local variable block for invSigma[k] */
>     /* priors for invSigma[k] */
>     tau ~ gamma( 1.0, 1.0 ); /* K x 1 vector of cluster-indexed precision parameters */
>     rho ~ uniform( 0, 1 ); /* K x 1 vector of cluster-indexed strength of correlation */
>     for( k in 1:K )
>     {
>       mu[k]         ~ normal( 0.0, 5.0 ); /* T x 1 cluster centers */
>
>     } /* end loop k over clusters */
>   } /* end construction of local variables, invSigma */
>
>
>   // prior for latent response, u_{i} ~ prod_{k=1}^{K}theta_k *N(u_{i},mu_k,Sigma_k)
>   for( i in 1:N ) /* by row of N x T, u */
>   {
>     real ps[K];
>     for( k in 1:K )
>     {
>       ps[k] <- log(theta[k]) + multi_normal_prec_log(u[i], mu[k], invSigma[k]);
>     }
>     increment_log_prob( log_sum_exp(ps) );
>   }
>
>   // prior for time-indexed fixed effects, P x T, Beta
>   // using separable covariance structure with PxP Lambda
>   // and TxT precision, Q (constructed as a CAR, RW(1))
>   /* sample parameters that compose PxP, Lambda and TxT Q */
>   {
>     /* TxT, Q <- tb * (D-rb*Omega) = CAR precision matrix */
>     //tb                        ~ gamma( 1, 1 );
>     rb                        ~ uniform( 0, 1 );
>
>     // prior on P x P covariance matrix, Lambda
>     corr_Lambda               ~ lkj_corr( 4 );
>     lam_tau                   ~ cauchy( 0, 5 );
>     // note: kron(Lambda,Q) \ equiv Q \kron Lambda, so T is slow and P is fast.
>     // results from stacking the columns of P x T, Beta into PT x 1, beta_long
>     z                         ~ normal( 0,1 );
>   } /* end local variable blocks for Q, Sigma_beta and Lbeta */
>
>
>   // observed response likelihood
>   { /* block to declare xb as a local variable */
>     matrix[N,T] xb;
>     xb    <- x * Beta; // N x P, x, times P x T, Beta
>     for( i in 1:N ) /* by row of y */
>     {
>       y[i] ~ normal( xb[i] + u[i], sigma_y[i] ); /* vectorized for T x 1 response, y[i] */
>     }
>   } /* end block to declare xb as a local variable */
>
>
> } /* end model{} block */
>
>
> On Tue, Jan 12, 2016 at 8:46 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I would say to try a very small positive value of init_r (like 0.1) but even then there is no guarantee that there will be sufficient numerical precision for ADVI to get going, much less whether the parameters really are close to multivariate normal in the unconstrained space.
>
>
> On Tuesday, January 12, 2016 at 6:54:57 PM UTC-5, tds151 wrote:
> Thx for the quick reply, Ben.  I hadn't thought about the point that initial values are generated for unconstrained parameters under mean-field Gaussian estimation.  I tried both limiting the range with init_r (e.g., init_r = 1) but receive the same error messages I specified in my first email.  Does the failure to generate acceptable initial values indicate that normal approximations for one or more of the parameters in the unconstrained space don't work?  Seems counterintuitive as my model is a mixture of Gaussians.  Is it common to have one's ADVI estimation fail on generation of the initial values?  I use weakly informative priors.  I'm not getting any traction by further tightening these priors - I get the same errors, not matter how informative I make the priors.  Lastly, it is a problem to use restricted specifications, such a cov_matrix and cholesky_factor_cov - I do get an "informational' message" that a cholesky_factor_cov in my model is ill-conditioned.  When I increase init_r to a relatively large value (init_r = 10), I then receive a  further lack of symmetry message for the cholesky_factor_cov matrix.
>
> I'm pretty well stuck as to how/whether to proceed with ADVI.
>
> Terrance
>
> On Tue, Jan 12, 2016 at 6:19 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> It is not currently possible to specify initial values for ADVI via rstan because the mechanism we use for sampling is not directly applicable since ADVI needs initial values for the normal variational approximation. You can however specify init_r to some value (it is 2 by default) to limit the range of the initial values in the variational approximation. I don't think the fact that you do Kronecker products or other operations make the evaluation of the log-posterior function too complicated, but it is a valid empirical question as to whether the parameters are approximately normal in the unconstrained space.
>
> Ben
>
>
> On Tuesday, January 12, 2016 at 6:00:38 PM UTC-5, tds151 wrote:
> Hi, I'm attempting to perform ADVI on a mixture model in specified in the attached file, dpmix_2.stan.  The model imposes the mixture distribution on observation-indexed random effects, rather than directly on the (multivariate) data.  The mixture probabilities are specified such that limiting mixture distribution is a Dirichlet process (which penalizes the number of clusters selected).  The number of dimensions is relatively small, so cluster-indexed covariance matrices are included to allow the data to learn dependence among the dimensions.  The dimensions index time, so an autocorrelated covariance structure (CAR) is used.  Each multivariate observation is drawn from a Gaussian with the mean defined as the sum of a fixed effects term and an observation-indexed random effects term.
>
> The attached file, syndata_vb_run.R uses draw_syndata_mix.R to generate synthetic data, then compiles the dpmix_2.stan to stanmodel object and performs ADVI estimation.
>
> I receive the following error message when running vb():
>
> Rejecting initial value:
>   Error evaluating the log probability at the initial value.
>
> I'm also informed that:
>    validate transformed params: Lbeta is not lower triangular; Lbeta[1,2]=1.62024e-315
>
> the object Lbeta is the cholesky of a separable covariance matrix composed from the kronecker product of two lower dimensional covariance matrices.  everything is declared as restricted; e.g., cov_matrix, cholesky_factor_cov.
>
> I'd appreciate your insight on the following questions:
> 1. Does this error message indicate that I should supply initial parameter values and, if so, how does one do that under vb() in rstan 2.9.0 (which i installed from github, yesterday)?
> -- it seems vb() inputs a stanmodel object, but no input field for initial values
>
> 2. I'm using 3 x 3 and 12 x 12 covariance and precision matrices, separately, and built into a 36 x 36 separable covariance structure using the kronecker product.  Is this not a good idea for ADVI?  Said differently, is this model just too complicated for ADVI (at this time)?  I had hoped that my twist on the mixture model included in the paper was relatively minor.
>
> 3. Are there other considerations I should be aware of when assessing whether my model is estimable under ADVI?
>
> Thank you for your help and expertise,
>
> Terrance.
>
>

> On Jan 14, 2016, at 5:32 PM, terrance savitsky <tds...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for the tips, Bob. I'm re-jiggering initial values and prior formulations as a model that estimates well under mean field vb() may not under NUTS. I was wondering whether you would offer any insights on whether any of my prior formulations are particularly bad. Yes, I know about the scaling issues, which defeated my previous attempts to estimate models in Stan with many levels of hierarchy.

I'm not the right person to ask about this. Maybe if
there's a more specific question than checking a very
complex looking program it might be easier for someone
else to answer.

Empirically, you want to check that the posteriors make
sense and aren't too sensitive to the priors (unless you
made the priors informative for a reason).

> Armadillo is a C++ linear algebra library made available for use in R programming with Rcpp via the package RcppArmadillo. It relies on the user's rblas, unlike RcppEigen used by Stan, but has easy-to-use syntax. My point was that Armadillo also allows for restrictive declarations, which it enforces, to either employ a speedier decomposition algorithm or to aid in numerical stability. So, for example, if one declares a matrix as lower triangular, it automatically zeros out the upper triangular elements. Stan, differently, checks and may produce an error if any of the upper triangular elements of a declared cholesky covariance matrix are non-zero within some precision, which sometimes happens for me due to numerical precision issues.

Eigen has that capability, too. And we have some
specialized operatiosn built in, but they all validate
their arguments rather than just providing views of them.

If you take a symmetric view of a matrix in Eigen, it ignores
above diagonal and duplicates below diagonal. We thought
telling users to pass in a lower-triangular matrix for
symmetric multiplication might be confusing, but we're looking
into things like this now going forward.

If there's something you think's going wrong in error
checking, let us know specifically what function for what
inputs and we can look into it.

- Bob
